stories.title: Work Underway on Las Vegas Airport Hangar, Office Space
stories.excerpt: Infrastructure developer and hangar keeper SR Aviation Infrastructure (SRAI), has broken ground on a $22 million project at Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (KLAS). SRAI acquired the 23-acre property, with 268,000 square feet of hangar space and 32,000 square feet of office space, in 2024. The company will demolish 14 small hangars totaling 61,000 square feet by year-end and replace them with three 25,000-square-foot hangars, equipped with ample office space and 30-foot-high doors capable of accommodating the latest ultra-long-range business jets. The hangars are suitable for corporations, high net worth individuals, and/or charter companies. One of the three hangars—slated for completion in the first quarter of 2028—has already been leased. While the KLAS facility was SRAI’s first, it has five others, three operational: Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport (KBZN) in Montana and San Antonio International Airport (KSAT), along with Las Vegas; and three under development in Montana, Denver and Long Island. The post Work Underway on Las Vegas Airport Hangar, Office Space appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SR Aviation breaks ground on $22M Las Vegas airport hangar project; one of three hangars pre-leased.
Project demolishes 61K SF small hangars, replaces with three 25K SF units targeting ultra-long-range jets.
SRAI operates three facilities (Bozeman, San Antonio, Las Vegas); three more under development in Denver, Montana, Long Island.
stories.summary: SR Aviation Infrastructure is demolishing 14 small hangars totaling 61,000 square feet at Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport and replacing them with three 25,000-square-foot hangars equipped for ultra-long-range business jets. The $22 million project, which breaks ground in 2025 and delivers first hangar in Q1 2028, has already secured one lease. SRAI operates five total facilities across Bozeman, San Antonio, and Las Vegas, with three more under development.
stories.impact: No material impact to multifamily development. Hangar and aviation infrastructure does not influence residential demand, supply, or construction feasibility in Las Vegas metro.

stories.title: Dwight Investment Management Provides $73M Refi for Reno’s Ballpark Apartments
stories.excerpt: Play ball! A joint venture between Bridge Investment Group and Pacific Development has scored $73 million of bridge debt to refinance its newly built Ballpark Apartments property in Reno, Nev., Commercial Observer has learned. Dwight Investment Management supplied the loan for the 368-unit complex that overlooks Greater Nevada Field, home of the Reno Aces, a Triple-A minor league affiliate of the Arizona Diamondbacks. Loan proceeds were used to fund an interest reserve and return equity to the borrower, according to Dwight, with Brandon Baksh, Tommy Ng and Talisse Thompson originating the refi. Located at 201 Evans Avenue, the five-story Ballpark Apartments debuted in early 2025. Its resident amenities include a swimming pool, a spa, a fitness center and a rooftop lounge. The 486,000-square-foot development has contributed to ongoing revitalization efforts in Reno, according to Dwight. Pacific Development acquired the land site for Ballpark Apartments in 2021 from Simon Property Group for $12 million, the Reno Gazette Journal previously reported. “Ballpark Apartments reflects our long-standing commitment to developing high-quality communities that contribute to the long-term vitality of the markets we serve,” Sean Murphy, founding partner of Pacific Development, said in a statement. “The financing puts us in an excellent position to continue building a brighter future for Downtown Reno.” Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dwight Investment Management closes $73M bridge refi for 368-unit Ballpark Apartments in Reno, completed early 2025.
Bridge Investment Group and Pacific Development JV refinancing newly built asset; proceeds fund interest reserve and equity return.
Property overlooks Greater Nevada Field (Reno Aces Triple-A); part of broader Reno downtown revitalization.
stories.summary: A Bridge Investment Group and Pacific Development joint venture refinanced the newly completed 368-unit Ballpark Apartments in Reno, Nevada with a $73 million bridge loan from Dwight Investment Management. The five-story, 486,000-square-foot property delivered in early 2025 and overlooks Greater Nevada Field, home of the Reno Aces. Loan proceeds funded an interest reserve and returned equity to the borrower.
stories.impact: Signals strong capital availability and lender confidence in Reno multifamily; fresh equity return on new construction suggests stabilized occupancy and rent achievement post-delivery. Entry of bridge capital at attractive rates supports forward underwriting assumptions for Reno infill development and confirms market momentum tied to downtown revitalization initiatives.

stories.title: The NYC Community Opportunity to Purchase Act Passed — Now What?
stories.excerpt: The New York City Council passed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA) on Thursday afternoon after six years of revisions and a mayoral veto. The law, passed 38-9 by City Council members, gives nonprofit organizations — with or without joint venture partners — first dibs on rent-stabilized buildings being sold. It aims to transfer some of the housing stock away from the private sector or for-profit landlords. The revised bill gives nonprofit buyers a leg up, requiring sellers to inform the New York City Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) when they intend to list a property so potential buyers can have 70 days to submit an offer. But one of the major changes in the bill gives the seller somewhat of an advantage: they can apply for an exemption arguing undue financial hardship. That’s something that is becoming more common for landlords of rent-stabilized properties, which are facing increasing costs and little relief, especially following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s controversial freeze on rent increases in this sector that went into effect Oct. 1. Additionally, COPA will only apply to properties dealing with a high number of violations from either HPD or the New York City Department of Buildings and those participating in a city remediation program. Mamdani was public in his support of the bill in May, so it is likely to be signed into law this time around. But the program may not be the breakthrough for nonprofit organizations that the City Council believes it could be. “Nonprofit buildings in many ways don’t pay property taxes and they’re still financially struggling, which goes to show you that this is as much of an expense problem as it is also a revenue problem,” Kenny Burgos, CEO of the New York Apartment Association, said in an interview with Commercial Observer. “We’ve just had this perfect storm of uncontrollable factors like interest rates and COVID, but the only controllable factors like government regulations and laws and
bullets: NYC Council passes Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA) 38-9 after six-year effort and mayoral veto override.
Law grants nonprofits 70-day right of first refusal on rent-stabilized sales; allows seller hardship exemptions.
Landlords facing frozen rents (October 2024) plus rising costs; exemption provision signals distress risk in RSA market.
stories.summary: New York City Council passed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA), requiring sellers of rent-stabilized buildings to notify HPD and give nonprofit organizations 70 days to match offers. However, the revised bill includes a seller-requested hardship exemption that allows opt-out of the requirement. The law comes as rent-stabilized landlords face a rent increase freeze and rising operational costs.
stories.impact: For multifamily developers, COPA narrows the buyer pool for rent-stabilized acquisition opportunities in NYC by prioritizing nonprofit bidders, raising acquisition costs and reducing deal velocity in the stabilized segment. Conversely, hardship exemptions and landlord distress from the rent freeze create potential for experienced for-profit developers to acquire distressed RSA properties at discounts—but only if they can compete with or partner alongside nonprofits. Market likely to fragment: newer market-rate inventory remains open to traditional development; older RSA stock faces nonprofit conversion, reducing future repositioning upside.

stories.title: Younger Partners Picks Up 260K-SF Terrell Retail Center
stories.excerpt: Younger Partners Investments (YPI) acquired the fully leased 260,876-square-foot power center, Crossroads at Terrell, at Interstate 20 and Spur 557 in Terrell. Younger Partners’ Kathy Permenter and Moody Younger represented the buyers. Institutional Property Advisors (IPA) Philip Levy and Marcus & Millichap’s Chris Gainey represented the seller, RealtyLink, LLC. Younger’s Micah Ashford added, “We began our pursuit of Crossroads at Terrell when we saw the Placer.ai data stating the destination ranked third among the state’s most visited retail destinations in 2025.” Located on 29 acres, Crossroads at Terrell, built between 2019 and 2024, features a diversified national tenant roster including Academy Sports + Outdoors, Hobby Lobby, Marshalls, Bealls, Ross Dress for Less, Petco, Ulta Beauty, Five Below, Buffalo Wild Wings, and other leading retailers. The shopping center is also located adjacent to the existing Buc-ee’s. IPA’s Adam Mengacci and Travis Headapohl arranged acquisition financing, comprised of a senior loan from a regional bank and a preferred equity investment from a national REIT. bullets: Younger Partners acquires fully leased 260.9K SF power center in Terrell, Texas (I-20 and Spur 557) for undisclosed price.

The 29-acre property features leading national tenants and ranked third among Texas retail destinations in 2025 foot traffic per Placer.ai. Acquisition financing included a senior loan from a regional bank and preferred equity from a national REIT.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. Retail power center acquisition does not drive residential demand, supply pipeline, or development feasibility in Terrell or broader Dallas-Fort Worth. However, retail destination ranking signals strong trade area traffic and consumer activity, which could indirectly support future mixed-use or multifamily development in Terrell if followed by population and employment in-migration.

stories.title: KKR Refis Brooklyn Apartments With $95M Loan
stories.excerpt: A joint venture involving Avery Hall Investments, Bridge Investment Group and Declaration Partners has sealed a $95 million loan to refinance a newly built multifamily property in Brooklyn’s Gowanus neighborhood, Commercial Observer has learned. KKR supplied the 10-year, fixed-rate loan for the sponsorship’s 17-story apartment building at 544 Carroll Street that was completed late last year. bullets: KKR closes $95M 10-year fixed-rate loan for 544 Carroll Street, Gowanus, Brooklyn; completed late 2024.
Avery Hall Investments, Bridge Investment Group, Declaration Partners JV refinances newly built 17-story apartment building.
Refi retires $71.1M past debt; demonstrates strong capital availability and lender confidence in Brooklyn infill.
stories.summary: A joint venture of Avery Hall Investments, Bridge Investment Group, and Declaration Partners refinanced the 544 Carroll Street apartment building in Brooklyn's Gowanus neighborhood with a $95 million 10-year fixed-rate loan from KKR. The 17-story property was completed in late 2024. The refinancing retired approximately $71.1 million of prior debt and was arranged by JLL.
stories.impact: Strong signal of capital confidence in Brooklyn neighborhoods undergoing revitalization. KKR's 10-year fixed-rate commitment on newly built Gowanus product at scale indicates investor appetite for next-phase development in the submarket. Gowanus rezoning and infrastructure investment (Superfund cleanup progress, transit) now attracting institutional long-term capital, reducing uncertainty for forward pipeline. Developers with shovel-ready Gowanus or adjacent Brooklyn infill sites should move quickly—window for acquisition and entitlement is open, and cap rate compression suggests pricing will tighten as more capital competes.

stories.title: Lehi, Utah Rental Community Trades for $130M
stories.excerpt: Mountain States Properties sold Seasons of Traverse, a 440-unit apartment community in Lehi, Utah, for $130 million. The sale marks the largest widely marketed multifamily transaction on record in Utah County. Cushman & Wakefield’s Kip Paul, Kevin Donner, Michael King, JT Redd, James Hunsinger, and Katie Goldberg represented seller Mountain States Properties in the transaction. The buyer was Weidner Apartment Homes. “The property attracted nearly 30 offers from institutional and private investors across the country — the depth and diversity of buyer interest underscored the rare opportunity to acquire 440 units in the heart of rapidly growing northern Utah County,” said Paul. Located at 4200 North Seasons View Drive, Seasons of Traverse Mountain is a grouping of four-story buildings, completed in 2014. It features 222 two-bedroom units, 168 one-bedroom units and 50 three-bedroom units. Lehi remains one of the fastest-growing markets in Utah. The post Lehi, Utah Rental Community Trades for $130M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Weidner Apartment Homes acquires Seasons of Traverse, 440-unit community in Lehi, Utah, for $130M.
Sale marks largest widely marketed multifamily transaction on record in Utah County; generated ~30 offers nationally.
Property completed 2014, features mix of one-, two-, three-bedroom units in four-story buildings; built in rapidly growing northern Utah County.
stories.summary: Mountain States Properties sold Seasons of Traverse, a 440-unit apartment community in Lehi, Utah, to Weidner Apartment Homes for $130 million, marking the largest widely marketed multifamily transaction on record in Utah County. The property, completed in 2014 and comprising four-story buildings, attracted nearly 30 offers from institutional and private investors across the country. It includes 222 two-bedroom, 168 one-bedroom, and 50 three-bedroom units.
stories.impact: Intense bidding for legacy (2014) multifamily asset in rapidly growing northern Utah County signals strong institutional demand for established communities in high-growth submarkets. Depth of buyer competition (30 offers) and record transaction size in Utah County indicate that the market has matured—national capital now views Lehi as trophy market. For developers: entry pricing on new development sites in Lehi/northern Utah County likely rising; value-add repositioning of older Class B assets is still competitive. Focus forward efforts on land assembly or Class A new construction to avoid pricing compression on secondary vintage product.

stories.title: Harrison Street, CP Group Trade Boca Raton Offices for $82.1M
stories.excerpt: Harrison Street and CP Group offloaded the One Boca Place office building for $78.88 million. The S. Florida Business Journal reports that Golden East Investor was the buyer. City National Bank of Florida provided an $82.1 million construction to the buyer. One Boca Place last traded for $76.35 million in 2014. The four-story office was built on the 7.75-acre site just west of Interstate 95 in 1986. It has 286,890 square feet of office space. It features a conference center, a café, a fitness center, and an on-site car wash. There is 75,900 square feet of space available for lease at One Boca Place at an asking rate of $52 per square foot. CP Group was part of a group that sold the Boca Raton Innovation Campus (BRIC) to Related Ross in September. And days later, CP Group sold Two Town Center, where it houses its headquarters. bullets: Harrison Street and CP Group sell One Boca Place office building to Golden East Investor for $78.88M.

The 286,890-square-foot four-story office, built in 1986 on 7.75 acres west of I-95, has 75,900 square feet of vacant space at an asking rate of $52 per square foot.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. Office asset transaction and CP Group portfolio liquidation do not signal residential demand or development opportunity. However, CP Group's exit from Boca Raton office and BRIC sale may indicate internal capital reallocation or portfolio repositioning; monitor for signals that proceeds are redirected to multifamily or mixed-use in South Florida.

stories.title: Grover Corlew Pays Nearly $70M for Fort Lauderdale Office Tower
stories.excerpt: Grover Corlew acquired 200 East Broward, a 21-story, 235,211-square-foot Class A office tower in downtown Fort Lauderdale, for $69.7 million. Banyan Street Capital was the seller. Banyan and Oaktree Capital Management bought the tower in 2017 for $81.5 million. Grover Corlew plans to invest an additional $20 million in improvements to the property over the next two years. Renovations will include the full modernization of the building’s elevator and main lobby, the addition of an amenity deck with a gym and conference facilities, and best-in-class tenant finishes.  JLL served as the selling broker, with Hermen Rodriguez and Ike Ojala handling the sale. JLL’s Paul Stasaitis handled the debt financing. BridgeInvest provided financing.  The acquisition adds to Grover Corlew’s investments throughout Broward County. In Fort Lauderdale, the firm is developing Mayla Cypress, a 312-unit luxury apartment community in the city’s Uptown Urban Village, within the Cypress Creek business corridor. The post Grover Corlew Pays Nearly $70M for Fort Lauderdale Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Grover Corlew acquires 200 East Broward, 21-story, 235K SF Class A office tower in downtown Fort Lauderdale, for $69.7M.
Grover Corlew plans $20M capital investment over two years; elevator, lobby, amenity deck, tenant finishes.
Grover Corlew developing Mayla Cypress, 312-unit luxury apartments in Fort Lauderdale Uptown Urban Village (Cypress Creek corridor).
stories.summary: Grover Corlew acquired 200 East Broward, a 21-story, 235,211-square-foot Class A office tower in downtown Fort Lauderdale, from Banyan Street Capital for $69.7 million. The purchase price represents a $11.8 million loss from Banyan and Oaktree Capital's 2017 acquisition price of $81.5 million. Grover Corlew plans to invest an additional $20 million in capital improvements, including elevator and lobby modernization, new amenity deck, and tenant finishes.
stories.impact: Grover Corlew's simultaneous office acquisition and apartment development in Fort Lauderdale signals conviction in downtown revitalization and mixed-use district activation. Office repositioning (Class A upgrade) and new luxury multifamily (Mayla Cypress, 312 units in Uptown Urban Village/Cypress Creek) indicate developer thesis that downtown office-to-residential conversion and nearby higher-density residential support each other. However, office acquisition at distressed price (loss vs. 2017) reflects ongoing office headwinds; monitor whether capital intensity of office CapEx (20M on $70M asset) compresses returns and diverts capital from residential development acceleration in Fort Lauderdale.

stories.title: Podcast: Reducing CRE Energy Costs with Physical AI, with R-Zero CEO Jennifer Nuckles

She previously served as EVP at SoFi and CMO at Zynga, and spent nearly a decade as a Global Business Lead at Clorox. She is a board member and chairperson of the American Lung Association and a trustee at UC Riverside. Based in San Francisco. bullets: R-Zero physical AI platform claims 20-40% HVAC energy savings with no major retrofit required.
CEO Jennifer Nuckles highlights Local Law 97 and building efficiency as NOI lever; regulatory tailwind.

stories.summary: R-Zero CEO Jennifer Nuckles discusses a physical AI platform that delivers 20-40% HVAC energy savings in existing buildings without major retrofits. The podcast highlights energy efficiency as a material NOI lever, particularly in response to NYC Local Law 97 and rising operating costs. R-Zero's model connects building data to optimize HVAC performance autonomously.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development underwriting for new construction. However, regulatory tightening (Local Law 97) and growing cost of ownership make energy efficiency a competitive advantage in asset positioning and tenant attraction. For developers: factor energy performance standards into new construction design and equipment selection to reduce long-term operating cost exposure and improve asset value retention. Existing portfolio owners face pressure to retrofit or adopt energy tech, potentially narrowing cap rates on inefficient legacy assets—opportunity for value-add developers to acquire and upgrade.

stories.title: Voya Provides $96M Refi for 1,461-Unit SoCal Portfolio
stories.excerpt: E&S Ring has secured refinancing from Voya Investment Management for a six-property multifamily portfolio in Southern California. Northmarq on Thursday announced the $95.8 million refinancing for the 1,461-unit portfolio. The firm’s Nathan Prouty, Andrew Slaton and John Holt facilitated the deal. The refinance covers existing debt across the portfolio, including four loans from Voya in 2007. The new financing is structured as six non-cross-collateralized loans, and includes a combination of fixed- and floating-rate debt, interest-only payments and prepayment provisions. Four properties are in Los Angeles neighborhoods, one is in Culver City, and the sixth is in Victorville. The portfolio includes the 168-unit Casa Granada and 183-unit Sunset Barrington Gardens in Brentwood; the 117-unit Meadows South in Culver City; the 400-unit Mountain Vista in Victorville; the 317-unit Rancho Los Feliz in Los Feliz; and the 276-unit Villa Vicente in Mid-Wilshire. Greater Los Angeles multifamily vacancy held at 4.5 percent through the first half of the year, while average rent remained slightly below the level from one year ago, according to Northmarq’s most recent numbers. Investment activity accelerated, with more than 40 percent more properties trading in the first half than during the same period in 2025. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Voya Investment Management closes $95.8M refi for E&S Ring six-property, 1,461-unit SoCal multifamily portfolio.
Portfolio includes four Los Angeles properties, one Culver City, one Victorville; non-cross-collateralized structure with fixed/floating mix.
Refi covers Voya loans from 2007; refinance at scale signals strong capital availability for stabilized LA/SoCal multifamily.
stories.summary: E&S Ring secured a $95.8 million refinancing from Voya Investment Management for a six-property, 1,461-unit multifamily portfolio across Southern California. The portfolio includes four properties in Los Angeles neighborhoods (Casa Granada, Sunset Barrington Gardens, Rancho Los Feliz, Villa Vicente), one in Culver City (Meadows South), and one in Victorville (Mountain Vista). The new financing is structured as six non-cross-collateralized loans with fixed- and floating-rate options, and refinances existing Voya debt from 2007.
stories.impact: Voya's willingness to refinance a 1,461-unit portfolio—including legacy assets originated in 2007—at scale signals confidence in stabilized Southern California multifamily and sustained capital availability for portfolio players. LA area multifamily vacancy at 4.5% supports strong debt underwriting. For developers: refinance wave and extended hold periods by institutional sponsors indicate limited near-term disposition activity in core LA/SoCal; acquisition opportunities for new projects will require either opportunistic distress purchases or targeting infill land/development-stage deals. Strong refinance market also suggests cap rates remain compressed, making new construction feasibility challenging unless rents outpace construction cost inflation.
